CONSERVATORSHIP OF AN ADULT — PETITION INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

THIS PETITION INFORMATION SHEET DESCRIBES A COURT PROCEEDING, NOT A PRIVATE DESIGNATION
A conservatorship over Pat Morgan, an adult, under California law is established only through an actual court proceeding under Probate Code Division 4, Part 3 — a filed petition, notice, an investigation, and a hearing that ends in a court order — not by a private agreement, family consensus, or the mere signing of this document. This is a genuinely different process from a power of attorney or advance health care directive, both of which are private, voluntary designations an adult makes for themself, in advance, while still able to do so; a conservatorship is instead a court-supervised proceeding brought about someone else, over their objection if necessary. California Probate Code § 1820(a) lists who may file the petition that starts that proceeding: the proposed conservatee themself, the proposed conservatee's spouse or domestic partner, a relative of the proposed conservatee, an interested state or local public entity, officer, or employee, or any other interested person or friend of the proposed conservatee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A petition for the appointment of a conservator may be filed by any of the following: (1) The proposed conservatee. (2) The spouse or domestic partner of the proposed conservatee. (3) A relative of the proposed conservatee. (4) Any interested state or local entity or agency of this state or any interested public officer or employee of this state or of a local public entity of this state. (5) Any other interested person or friend of the proposed conservatee."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1820(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1820(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1820.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that an adult conservatorship is created only through an actual court proceeding, and of who may file the petition that starts it — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This document is informational: it describes the statutory conservatorship petition process and does not itself establish a conservatorship, appoint anyone as conservator, or determine that the proposed conservatee lacks capacity for any purpose; only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, investigation, and hearing process can do that. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 1820(a)); no additional independent source was found for the list of persons who may petition. Section 1820(b) and (c), addressing petitions filed during a proposed conservatee's minority and a bar on most creditor-filed petitions, are not covered by this clause.

CONSERVATOR OF THE PERSON, CONSERVATOR OF THE ESTATE — TWO DISTINCT, SEVERABLE KINDS OF CONSERVATORSHIP
California law recognizes two distinct kinds of adult conservatorship, and a petition may seek either or both for Pat Morgan. A conservator of the person may be appointed for a person who is "unable to provide properly for his or her personal needs for physical health, food, clothing, or shelter" — authority over day-to-day care and living arrangements. A conservator of the estate may be appointed for a person who "is substantially unable to manage his or her own financial resources or resist fraud or undue influence," with the added statutory caution that "[s]ubstantial inability may not be proved solely by isolated incidents of negligence or improvidence" — authority over money and property instead of personal care. A conservator of the person and estate may be appointed where both descriptions apply, but the two are legally severable: a court petition, and a resulting court order, may establish one without the other. Whichever type is sought, the standard of proof for the appointment is clear and convincing evidence.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A conservator of the person may be appointed for a person who is unable to provide properly for his or her personal needs for physical health, food, clothing, or shelter, except as provided for the person as described in subdivision (b) or (c) of Section 1828.5."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1801(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1801(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1801.)
  "A conservator of the estate may be appointed for a person who is substantially unable to manage his or her own financial resources or resist fraud or undue influence, except as provided for that person as described in subdivision (b) or (c) of Section 1828.5. Substantial inability may not be proved solely by isolated incidents of negligence or improvidence."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1801(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1801(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1801.)
  "A conservator of the person and estate may be appointed for a person described in subdivisions (a) and (b)."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1801(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1801(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1801.)
  "The standard of proof for the appointment of a conservator pursuant to this section shall be clear and convincing evidence."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1801(e) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1801(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1801.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the two distinct, severable types of adult conservatorship recognized under California law and the standard of proof that applies to each — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This clause cites four subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1801(a), (b), (c), and (e)); no additional independent source beyond § 1801 itself was found for the two-types distinction, the severability of the two types, or the clear-and-convincing standard of proof. Subdivision (d) of the same section — the limited conservatorship for a developmentally disabled adult — is deliberately not quoted in this clause; it is addressed on its own in this document's companion clause because it is a narrower, separately governed category that this document does not treat as interchangeable with a general conservatorship of the person or estate.

WHAT THE PETITION MUST SAY — INCLUDING ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED AND WHO MUST BE NAMED
The petition to appoint a conservator for Pat Morgan must request appointment for the person, the estate, or both; specify the proposed conservator's and proposed conservatee's names, addresses, and telephone numbers; and state the reasons a conservatorship is necessary. Unless the petitioner or proposed conservator is a bank or trust company, supplemental information must also address, among other categories, the proposed conservatee's inability to provide for physical health, food, clothing, or shelter; the nature of the proposed conservatee's residence; alternatives to conservatorship that were considered and why they were not suitable — expressly including supported decision-making agreements, powers of attorney, advance health care directives, and health care surrogate designations; health or social services provided in the preceding year; and the proposed conservatee's substantial inability to manage financial resources or resist fraud or undue influence. So far as known to the petitioner or proposed conservator, the petition must also set forth the names and addresses of the proposed conservatee's spouse or domestic partner and relatives within the second degree.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The petition shall request that a conservator be appointed for the person or estate, or both, shall specify the name, address, and telephone number of the proposed conservator and the name, address, and telephone number of the proposed conservatee, and state the reasons why a conservatorship is necessary. Unless the petitioner or proposed conservator is a bank or other entity authorized to conduct the business of a trust company, the petitioner or proposed conservator shall also file supplemental information as to why the appointment of a conservator is required. The supplemental information to be submitted shall include a brief statement of facts addressed to each of the following categories: (A) The inability of the proposed conservatee to properly provide for their own needs for physical health, food, clothing, or shelter. (B) The location and nature of the proposed conservatee's residence and the ability of the proposed conservatee to live in the residence while under conservatorship. (C) Alternatives to conservatorship considered by the petitioner or proposed conservator and reasons why those alternatives are not suitable... Those alternatives include, but are not limited to, all of the following: (i) Supported decisionmaking agreements, as defined in Section 21001 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. (ii) Powers of Attorney set forth in Division 4.5 (commencing with Section 4000). (iii) Advanced Health Care Directives set forth in Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 4670) of Part 2 of Division 4.7. (iv) Designations of a health care surrogate as set forth in Section 4711. (D) Health or social services provided to the proposed conservatee during the year immediately preceding the filing of the petition, when the petitioner or proposed conservator has information as to those services. (E) The substantial inability of the proposed conservatee to manage their own financial resources, or to resist fraud or undue influence."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1821(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1821(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1821.)
  "The petition shall set forth, so far as they are known to the petitioner or proposed conservator, the names and addresses of the spouse or domestic partner, and of the relatives of the proposed conservatee within the second degree."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1821(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1821(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1821.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the required contents of a California conservatorship petition — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1821(a)(1) and § 1821(b)); no additional independent source beyond § 1821 itself was found for these requirements. This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: on the actual statutory text, § 1821 does not require the petition to include a capacity declaration from a licensed physician or other qualified professional, and no such physician-declaration requirement was located anywhere in § 1821. The petition-stage requirement that exists instead is the supplemental-information showing quoted above. The actual mechanism that brings a treating physician's or other health care provider's input into the case is a separate one, described in this document's companion clause on the court investigator: under § 1826(a)(9), it is the court investigator — not the petitioner — who is required to gather and review the proposed conservatee's relevant medical reports as part of the mandatory investigation, after the petition is filed.

THE COURT INVESTIGATOR'S MANDATORY INDEPENDENT INVESTIGATION AND INTERVIEW
Regardless of whether Pat Morgan attends the hearing, a court investigator must personally interview Pat Morgan, along with all petitioners, all proposed conservators who are not petitioners, and Pat Morgan's spouse or registered domestic partner and close relatives. As part of that same investigation, the court investigator must inform Pat Morgan of the contents of the petition, of the nature, purpose, and effect of the proceeding, and of the right to oppose the petition, to attend the hearing, to have the matter tried by jury, to be represented by legal counsel, and to have legal counsel appointed by the court if not otherwise represented. The investigator must also gather and review relevant medical reports regarding the proposed conservatee from the proposed conservatee's primary care physician and other relevant mental and physical health care providers, and must report the findings to the court in writing at least five days before the hearing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Regardless of whether the proposed conservatee attends the hearing, the court investigator shall do all of the following: (1) Conduct the following interviews: (A) The proposed conservatee personally. (B) All petitioners and all proposed conservators who are not petitioners. (C) The proposed conservatee's spouse or registered domestic partner and relatives within the first degree... (2) Inform the proposed conservatee of the contents of the petition and citation, of the nature, purpose, and effect of the proceeding, and of the right of the proposed conservatee to oppose the petition, to attend the hearing on the petition, to have the matter of the establishment of the conservatorship tried by jury, to be represented by legal counsel, and to have legal counsel appointed by the court if not otherwise represented by legal counsel."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1826(a)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1826(a)(1), (2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1826.)
  "(9) Gather and review relevant medical reports regarding the proposed conservatee from the proposed conservatee's primary care physician and other relevant mental and physical health care providers. (10) Report to the court in writing, at least five days before the hearing, concerning all of the foregoing..."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1826(a)(9)-(10) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1826(a)(9), (10) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1826.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real, independent, pre-appointment investigation and interview requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1826(a)(1)-(2) and § 1826(a)(9)-(10)); no additional independent source beyond § 1826 itself was found for these requirements. This investigation requirement does not apply, under § 1826(d), to a proposed conservatee who has personally executed the petition or who has nominated their own conservator, if that proposed conservatee attends the hearing — an exception this clause does not otherwise describe.

THE PROPOSED CONSERVATEE'S RIGHTS AT THE HEARING
Before a conservatorship over Pat Morgan may be established, the court must inform Pat Morgan that the establishment of a conservatorship is a legal adjudication of an inability to properly provide for personal needs or to manage financial resources, or both, and of its effect on Pat Morgan's basic rights. The court must also inform Pat Morgan of the right to oppose the proceeding, to have the matter tried by jury, to be represented by legal counsel of Pat Morgan's own choosing, and to have legal counsel appointed by the court if not otherwise represented by legal counsel. Separately, the court is required to hear and determine the matter of establishing the conservatorship according to the law and procedure that governs the trial of civil actions, including trial by jury if demanded by the proposed conservatee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The proposed conservatee has the right to oppose the proceeding, to have the matter of the establishment of the conservatorship tried by jury, to be represented by legal counsel if the proposed conservatee so chooses, and to have legal counsel appointed by the court if not otherwise represented by legal counsel."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1828(a)(6) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1828(a)(6) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1828.)
  "The court shall hear and determine the matter of the establishment of the conservatorship according to the law and procedure relating to the trial of civil actions, including trial by jury if demanded by the proposed conservatee."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1827 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1827 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1827.)

These citations are two different code sections (§ 1828(a)(6) and § 1827); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. Section 1828 also requires the court to inform the proposed conservatee of several other matters not covered by this clause, including the identity of the proposed conservator and, for an allegedly developmentally disabled adult, the specific effects of each limitation requested; and § 1828(c) excuses this requirement altogether where the proposed conservatee is absent from, and not required to attend, the hearing under § 1825.

LIMITED CONSERVATORSHIP FOR A DEVELOPMENTALLY DISABLED ADULT IS A DIFFERENT, NARROWER CATEGORY
California law separately provides for a limited conservatorship of the person or estate, or both, for a developmentally disabled adult — a genuinely different and narrower category from the general conservatorship described in the rest of this document, not an interchangeable label for the same thing. A limited conservatorship "may be utilized only as necessary to promote and protect the well-being of the individual, shall be designed to encourage the development of maximum self-reliance and independence of the individual, and shall be ordered only to the extent necessitated by the individual's proven mental and adaptive limitations," and the limited conservatee "shall not be presumed to be incompetent and shall retain all legal and civil rights except those which by court order have been designated as legal disabilities and have been specifically granted to the limited conservator." Consistent with that narrower scope, a limited conservator's default authority over the limited conservatee's person is confined to care, custody, control, and securing appropriate habilitation, treatment, training, education, and social or vocational services — the broader powers a general conservator of the person can hold are, for a limited conservator, available only if specifically requested in the petition and granted by the court's order.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A limited conservator of the person or of the estate, or both, may be appointed for a developmentally disabled adult. A limited conservatorship may be utilized only as necessary to promote and protect the well-being of the individual, shall be designed to encourage the development of maximum self-reliance and independence of the individual, and shall be ordered only to the extent necessitated by the individual's proven mental and adaptive limitations. The conservatee of the limited conservator shall not be presumed to be incompetent and shall retain all legal and civil rights except those which by court order have been designated as legal disabilities and have been specifically granted to the limited conservator."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1801(d) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1801(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1801.)
  "(1) The limited conservator has the care, custody, and control of the limited conservatee. (2) The limited conservator shall secure for the limited conservatee those habilitation or treatment, training, education, medical and psychological services, and social and vocational opportunity as appropriate and as will assist the limited conservatee in the development of maximum self-reliance and independence."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 2351.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 2351.5(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=2351.5.)

These citations are two different code sections (§ 1801(d) and § 2351.5(a)); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. This document addresses only the general conservatorship of the person and of the estate described in its other clauses; it does not describe, and should not be read as a stand-in for, the limited conservatorship petition process itself, which carries its own additional procedural requirements not covered here — including a regional center assessment and report under § 1827.5, and the court's specific findings on adaptive functioning and capacity under § 1828.5 — that this document does not address.

PROPOSED CONSERVATOR — INFORMATION AND DECLARATION IN SUPPORT OF PETITION
I, Jordan Lee, am the person proposed to serve as conservator of Pat Morgan, an adult. I state that my relationship to Pat Morgan is: adult child. The conservatorship sought is: conservator of the person and estate (for example, conservator of the person, conservator of the estate, or conservator of the person and estate). This declaration provides background information for use with an actual petition for appointment of a conservator, to be filed in the California probate court under Probate Code Division 4, Part 3. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not appoint, authorize, or confirm Jordan Lee — or anyone else — as Pat Morgan's conservator, and it does not itself adjudicate Pat Morgan's capacity for any purpose. Only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, investigation, and hearing process described in this document can actually establish a conservatorship or appoint a conservator.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT BLOCK — CONSERVATORSHIP PETITION INFORMATION SHEET
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

expectedJSON.body: Before a conservatorship over Pat Morgan may be established, the court must inform Pat Morgan that the establishment of a conservatorship is a legal adjudication of an inability to properly provide for personal needs or to manage financial resources, or both, and of its effect on Pat Morgan's basic rights. The court must also inform Pat Morgan of the right to oppose the proceeding, to have the matter tried by jury, to be represented by legal counsel of Pat Morgan's own choosing, and to have legal counsel appointed by the court if not otherwise represented by legal counsel. Separately, the court is required to hear and determine the matter of establishing the conservatorship according to the law and procedure that governs the trial of civil actions, including trial by jury if demanded by the proposed conservatee.

citations.quote: The proposed conservatee has the right to oppose the proceeding, to have the matter of the establishment of the conservatorship tried by jury, to be represented by legal counsel if the proposed conservatee so chooses, and to have legal counsel appointed by the court if not otherwise represented by legal counsel.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific rights a proposed conservatee has before and at the hearing on a conservatorship petition — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. These citations are two different code sections (§ 1828(a)(6) and § 1827); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. Section 1828 also requires the court to inform the proposed conservatee of several other matters not covered by this clause, including the identity of the proposed conservator and, for an allegedly developmentally disabled adult, the specific effects of each limitation requested; and § 1828(c) excuses this requirement altogether where the proposed conservatee is absent from, and not required to attend, the hearing under § 1825.

expectedJSON.body: California law separately provides for a limited conservatorship of the person or estate, or both, for a developmentally disabled adult — a genuinely different and narrower category from the general conservatorship described in the rest of this document, not an interchangeable label for the same thing. A limited conservatorship "may be utilized only as necessary to promote and protect the well-being of the individual, shall be designed to encourage the development of maximum self-reliance and independence of the individual, and shall be ordered only to the extent necessitated by the individual's proven mental and adaptive limitations," and the limited conservatee "shall not be presumed to be incompetent and shall retain all legal and civil rights except those which by court order have been designated as legal disabilities and have been specifically granted to the limited conservator." Consistent with that narrower scope, a limited conservator's default authority over the limited conservatee's person is confined to care, custody, control, and securing appropriate habilitation, treatment, training, education, and social or vocational services — the broader powers a general conservator of the person can hold are, for a limited conservator, available only if specifically requested in the petition and granted by the court's order.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1801(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A limited conservator of the person or of the estate, or both, may be appointed for a developmentally disabled adult. A limited conservatorship may be utilized only as necessary to promote and protect the well-being of the individual, shall be designed to encourage the development of maximum self-reliance and independence of the individual, and shall be ordered only to the extent necessitated by the individual's proven mental and adaptive limitations. The conservatee of the limited conservator shall not be presumed to be incompetent and shall retain all legal and civil rights except those which by court order have been designated as legal disabilities and have been specifically granted to the limited conservator.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2351.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (1) The limited conservator has the care, custody, and control of the limited conservatee. (2) The limited conservator shall secure for the limited conservatee those habilitation or treatment, training, education, medical and psychological services, and social and vocational opportunity as appropriate and as will assist the limited conservatee in the development of maximum self-reliance and independence.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a limited conservatorship for a developmentally disabled adult is a distinct, narrower statutory category from a general conservatorship — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. These citations are two different code sections (§ 1801(d) and § 2351.5(a)); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. This document addresses only the general conservatorship of the person and of the estate described in its other clauses; it does not describe, and should not be read as a stand-in for, the limited conservatorship petition process itself, which carries its own additional procedural requirements not covered here — including a regional center assessment and report under § 1827.5, and the court's specific findings on adaptive functioning and capacity under § 1828.5 — that this document does not address.
